value.text: Lucie police officers continued monitoring flooded neighborhoods and roads Tuesday morning, helping motorists and responding to calls for service as water levels began to recede in some areas. Lucie Police Department said it extended patrol shifts overnight to keep additional officers available to respond to emergencies. Officers were assessing roadways and neighborhoods at daybreak to identify hazards and determine the extent of the flooding. Aerial footage shared by the department showed significant flooding near SW Savage Boulevard, SW Fairgreen Road and SW Salvatierra Boulevard, where water had spread across residential streets and surrounding areas. Flooding was also affecting roadways and neighborhoods near Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard, as well as Torino Parkway, NW California Boulevard and NW Peacock Boulevard. Police said standing water made travel hazardous in those areas and urged motorists to stay off flooded roads. See also: Flooded roads complicate trip to Port St. Lucie polls; Legacy High School site is open The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office drone team is working with the St. Lucie County Fire District to conduct home checks in the Creekside community. Officers continued working throughout the city to assist residents, help stranded motorists, respond to calls and monitor areas affected by rising water. Police asked people to stay home if possible and allow emergency crews to assist those in need. Roads that are flooded, barricaded or significantly impacted Police reported flooding or barricades at these locations: Port St. Lucie Boulevard at Aviation Avenue Northbound Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Dalton Boulevard to Gatlin Boulevard Selvitz Road from Midway Road to Peachtree Boulevard Peachtree Boulevard Westmoreland Boulevard in front of The Anchorage Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard St. Lucie West Boulevard Volusia Drive from Blanton Boulevard to Torino Parkway California Boulevard in front of Fire Station 14 Country Club Estates of St. Lucie West Northbound Cashmere Boulevard Roads where water is receding or has cleared Police said water was beginning to recede on Lennard Road at Melaleuca Boulevard, Hillmoor Drive in front of HCA St. Lucie Medical Center and near the 1700 block, and Village Green Drive. Vehicles could pass on those roads, but four disabled vehicles on Lennard Road were awaiting removal. Flooding had subsided on Becker Road from Hallmark Street to Savona Boulevard, Darwin Boulevard and College Park Road. Several disabled vehicles remained on Becker and Darwin. Flooding had also cleared on Darwin Boulevard at Fifer Avenue, where two disabled vehicles remained. Rosser Boulevard had cleared, but SW Rosser Road at SW Paar Drive and SW Delos Drive remained flooded and impassable. Police reported no flooding on Airoso Boulevard from Lakehurst Boulevard to Eyerly Avenue, though several disabled vehicles in the county jurisdiction were awaiting removal. One disabled vehicle in a turn lane at Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Airoso Boulevard was not significantly impeding traffic. The department cautioned that conditions could change quickly, especially if more rain falls. Police urged drivers to avoid flooded roads, never drive through standing water and stay home unless travel is necessary. Turn Around, Don’t Drown, the department reminded residents. Call 911 to report downed power lines, fallen trees, road obstructions or other hazards that pose an immediate danger.

Susan Collins was vandalized in the hours leading up to Tuesday's election, her office said. It was the second reported act of vandalism at her Biddeford office.Officials have not said if anyone has been arrested or charged in connection to the incident. Collins' office released a photo indicating someone sprayed "BLOOD ON HER HANDS" in red paint."This is another incident in a series and the second attempt at our Biddeford office to intimidate the Senator and her staff. These tactics are disturbing, but not effective. Our staff is undeterred and on the job," Collins' chief of staff, Katie Brown, said in a statement.RELATED STORY | All eyes on Maine as critical Senate race draws closerCollins is in the midst of a tight reelection bid against Democrat Troy Jackson. Several polls in recent days have shown Jackson opening a narrow lead over Collins. She is seeking a sixth term in the Senate. Even in years when Maine has favored Democrats, Collins has won reelection by comfortable margins.For Republicans to retain control of the Senate, Collins' reelection is seen as imperative. With President Donald Trump's approval rating slowly declining, Collins has sought to distance herself from Trump in recent months.She has reminded voters that she was among seven Republicans who voted to convict Trump in his second impeachment trial in 2021.RELATED STORY | Americans head to polls in high-stakes 2026 midterm elections

If election season is causing stress, you're not alone.A survey from LifeStance Health found that 70% of Americans are experiencing at least some stress or anxiety about the midterm elections. Gen Z and millennials were more likely to report being stressed by the election. Only about one-third of respondents said they had a plan in place to protect their mental health on election night.About 37% said they are dreading having political conversations during the upcoming holiday season.RELATED STORY | How officials are preparing for Election Day disruptions — including from TrumpMental health experts recommend limiting how often you check election news, getting regular exercise and focusing on things you can control.Concerns extend beyond voters. Growing attention is being paid to the mental health of election workers, who have faced heavy workloads, public criticism and, in some cases, harassment and threats.The Carter Center has developed a mental well-being guide to help election officials recognize trauma, build resilience and access mental health support.The organization says prolonged stress can have serious effects on both physical and mental health.RELATED STORY | Election Day deals include free doughnuts and rides to the polls

If you're looking for more than just a free sticker on Election Day, shopping local may come with some extra perks.Federal law prohibits offering rewards in exchange for voting, but many businesses are providing giveaways and discounts to anyone who walks through the door.Krispy Kreme is offering a free Original Glazed doughnut to customers on Election Day. All you need to do is say you voted.RELATED STORY | In-person early voting hits record pace for midtermsIf you're facing a long wait at the polls, free pizza could be on the menu. Pizza to the Polls, a nonprofit and nonpartisan organization, delivers pizza from local restaurants to voters waiting in line.To request a delivery, visit polls.pizza, upload a photo of the line and provide your location.

Election Day is here, and voters in Port St. Lucie are heading to the polls Tuesday to decide who will lead one of Florida’s fastest-growing cities for the next four years. Incumbent Mayor Shannon Marti n is facing challenger Steven Giordano in a runoff election after neither candidate secured a majority of the vote in August. The race comes as residents continue to raise concerns about rapid growth, traffic congestion, infrastructure improvements, development and taxpayer spending. Meanwhile, widespread flooding across St. Lucie County has forced election officials to temporarily relocate several polling places ahead of Tuesday’s vote. Where the mayoral race stands Martin finished first in the August primary with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22%. Eric Strazzeri, who finished third with 17.07%, was eliminated from the race. That leaves approximately 6,700 voters who supported Strazzeri in August potentially playing a key role in deciding the outcome of Tuesday’s election. Both candidates have spent the months leading up to Election Day making their case to residents about the future of Port St. Martin is campaigning on her record, pointing to infrastructure improvements and roadwork already underway. Giordano, a longtime Port St. Lucie resident, business owner and former deputy, has called for slowing development until infrastructure can catch up with the city’s rapid growth. He has also called for a new traffic study. The candidates have different visions for how the city should use its land and approach future development. We already have 50 something parks here in Port St Lucie, we didn’t need another 23 acre park or 26 acre park in Tradition, lets utilize that space better, Giordano told CBS12 News. Martin has defended the city’s investments in parks and recreational spaces, saying they reflect what residents have requested. We have developed amazing parks in this city, our residents have asked for that and we have delivered on that and really its about what our residents tell us that they want, Martin said. The two also differ on plans involving a proposed soccer stadium and efforts to create a downtown destination with restaurants, shopping and entertainment. The winner will help shape the city’s future as Port St. Lucie continues to experience significant population growth. Trash collection also on the ballot Beyond the mayoral race, Port St. Lucie voters will also weigh in on another issue that has generated debate across the city: trash collection . Residents are being asked whether they support increasing residential trash pickup from once a week to twice a week at an additional cost. The proposal would increase the city’s annual solid waste assessment by at least $131 beginning in 2028, with additional increases expected in subsequent years. The additional pickup would apply to household garbage, not recycling, yard waste or bulk collection. The ballot question is nonbinding, meaning the results will help city leaders gauge public opinion, but the City Council will ultimately decide whether to move forward with the change. Flooding forces changes to Election Day polling locations As voters head to the polls Tuesday, several polling locations across St. Lucie County have been temporarily relocated because of flooding and unsafe road conditions. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced the changes Monday, saying the relocations are intended to ensure voters have safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Precinct 51 Disabled American Veterans Hall New location: Port St. Lucie Community Center (Precinct 45) Address: 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984 Access from Airoso Boulevard. Lucie West Centennial High School New location: Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence Address: 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34986 Access from Peacock Boulevard. Lewis Library New location: Tradition Town Hall Address: 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987 Precinct 92 The Brennity at Tradition New location: Tradition Town Hall Address: 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987 Election officials are encouraging voters to verify their assigned polling locations before leaving home because additional changes may be necessary as flooding conditions evolve. For the latest updates, voters can visit www.stlucievotes.gov or contact the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500. State of emergency declared amid widespread flooding The polling location changes come after days of heavy rainfall left roadways flooded and impassable across parts of St. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and infrastructure. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways. Lucie police have also extended shifts for officers to provide additional assistance as crews monitor flooding and respond to calls for service. According to the city, several major roadways were closed as of Monday evening, including the intersection of California and Savona boulevards and Port St. Lucie Boulevard at Aviation Avenue. Officials are urging residents to check the latest road conditions before traveling and to avoid driving around barricades or through standing water. Lucie County public schools, county government offices and courthouses are closed Tuesday because of the weather. Polling locations are scheduled to remain operational, including city facilities being used for voting. What voters need to know Polls are open Tuesday, Nov. Voters should confirm their assigned precinct, especially if their normal polling location has been affected by flooding. Election Day voters must cast their ballots at their assigned polling location. For information about precincts, voting requirements and election updates, visit www.stlucievotes.gov. CBS12 News will continue tracking the Port St. Lucie mayoral race and local election results throughout Election Day. This is a developing story.

Lucie County officials are urging residents to stay off the roads unless travel is necessary, as significant rainfall and flooding affect the area. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and critical infrastructure. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said numerous roads are flooded or impassable, with more rain expected through Monday night and Tuesday. Deputies and other personnel remain on duty and are coordinating with the Emergency Operations Center, the agency said. See also: NTSB: Learjet crew reported ice, turbulence before deadly Florida crash The sheriff’s office urged residents to stay home, never drive through floodwaters, and avoid moving or driving around barricades and road-closure signs. Residents should also stay away from downed power lines and standing water near electrical equipment, and monitor official sources for weather alerts and road updates. Lucie County Public Schools , county government offices and courthouses will be closed Tuesday, Nov. The agency thanked deputies, dispatchers, emergency personnel, and community partners responding to the conditions and urged residents to look out for their neighbors.

As Americans head to the polls on Election Day, affordability remains one of the top issues on voters' minds. Consumer spending has remained relatively strong despite higher prices, but shoppers and retailers alike are still grappling with uncertainty surrounding inflation, tariffs and changing shopping habits. Brett Rose, retail expert and CEO of United National Consumer Suppliers, said the uncertainty is making it harder for retailers to predict what consumers will buy months from now. "Anytime somebody in DC utters the word tariff right now, there's so much consumer concern and consumer uncertainty, which then translates to retail inventory concerns," Rose said. When retailers cannot accurately forecast demand, it affects both inventory decisions and pricing strategies. Shift toward regional suppliers Rose explained that many retailers are increasingly turning to nontraditional suppliers and looking for merchandise that is already available closer to home. "A lot less stuff coming out of the Far East because they need to find goods that are on the ground," Rose said. The strategy allows retailers to reduce risk and avoid being stuck with products that consumers may not ultimately purchase. It also helps businesses react more quickly in a rapidly changing market. Waiting for tariff refunds Another question facing retailers involves billions of dollars in tariff refunds being returned to importers by the federal government. But Rose said consumers should not expect those refunds to directly translate into lower prices at the checkout counter. RELATED STORY | Strong growth and inflation paints mixed picture of economy days before midterms"A lot of retailers are pushing back on suppliers and saying, 'Great. Glad you're getting the money back. When's our check coming?'" Rose said. Still, he said shoppers may be able to benefit indirectly by paying attention to off-price retailers. When companies overestimate demand and end up with excess inventory, they often sell those products to discount chains such as TJ Maxx, Dollar Tree, and Five Below. "There's a surplus of goods in the market. Off-price retailers take advantage of it," Rose said. "That's where the consumer benefits the most." Buying cycle gets shorter As economic concerns remain front and center on Election Day, Rose said retailers are already adapting to volatility regardless of what happens at the polls. One major shift is a shorter buying cycle. Instead of purchasing products 10 to 12 months in advance, retailers are increasingly buying inventory closer to when it will be sold. RELATED STORY | Midterm elections pit Iowans’ economic struggles against conservative values"You buy Christmas in January. You can't predict in a volatile consumer market what they're going to sell in December and January at the start of the year," Rose said. "A lot of traditional retailers, their buying process has become more like an off-price retailer." The changes, he said, reflect a retail industry that is increasingly focused on flexibility as it navigates an uncertain economic landscape.

Voting is underway in the 2026 midterm elections as Americans decide whether Republicans should retain control of all three branches of government.All 435 House seats and 35 of the Senate's 100 seats are on the ballot Tuesday. While most projections show Democrats regaining control of the House, the Senate remains less certain. Republicans can afford to lose three seats and still maintain control.In addition to federal races, voters in 36 states will choose governors. Many states also have ballot measures covering issues ranging from voting rights to school funding.Scripps News will provide live coverage throughout the day, with special coverage starting at 6 p.m.The first polls close at 6 p.m. Tuesday in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. In Kentucky, the 6th Congressional District could provide an early indication of where the night is headed for both parties.The Cook Political Report lists the district among 18 true tossup House races. The district, which includes the Lexington metropolitan area, has been represented by Republican Rep. Barr is leaving the House as he seeks election to Kentucky's U.S. Senate seat.RELATED STORY | In-person early voting hits record pace for midtermsIn 2024, Barr won the district by a 63%-37% margin. But the district has shown a willingness to support candidates from both parties. Andy Beshear carried the district in 2023, receiving about 60% of the vote there.This year, Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado.Among Senate races, Ohio could provide one of the earliest indicators of Democrats' chances of reclaiming the chamber. Polls there close at 7:30 p.m.The Ohio Senate race is one of two special elections this year. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown are competing to serve the final two years of the term won by Vice President JD Vance in 2022.Recent polls have shown Brown holding a narrow lead. Ohio is among the states Democrats likely must win if they hope to gain the four seats needed to reclaim the Senate.The 2026 midterm elections shattered early-voting records for a midterm cycle. The University of Florida's Election Lab reports that 58.9 million Americans have already cast ballots. If turnout resembles 2022 levels, that total would account for more than half of all votes cast.In recent elections, early voting has tended to favor Democrats, while Election Day voting has generally favored Republicans.There are signs Democrats performed better in early voting this year than in previous elections.In Ohio, for example, registered Democrats accounted for 27% of early votes, compared with 25% for Republicans. Unaffiliated voters made up the largest share.By comparison, registered Democrats accounted for just 17% of the state's early vote in 2024. However, Ohio has remained a reliably Republican state in recent federal elections and voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump in 2024.

Both Okeechobee County and Martin County Public Schools will be closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, as flooding and severe weather continue to create unsafe travel conditions across the region. MARTIN COUNTY SCHOOLS CLOSED All Martin County School District-operated schools will be closed Tuesday, which will also include all after-school activities. School officials said in a Facebook post that conditions vary significantly across the region, with some communities experiencing serious flooding and difficult travel conditions. The district said many of its employees and families live outside Martin County and commute into the county each day. Those conditions in neighboring communities played an important role in the decision to close schools. Throughout Monday, the district received reports of employees and families driving through floodwaters to get home, abandoning vehicles because of impassable roads and making alternate overnight accommodations because they could not safely remain in their homes. Officials said they also considered whether employees would be able to safely travel to and from campuses and whether schools would have enough staff and resources to safely support students throughout the day. The district said the decision follows Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' declaration of a state of emergency covering Martin County and surrounding counties. "We encourage everyone to use caution and prioritize their safety as conditions continue to affect our region," the district said. Families are being asked to monitor the Martin County School District's website and social media accounts for additional updates. OKEECHOBEE COUNTY SCHOOLS CLOSED Okeechobee County district officials announced Monday evening that lingering floodwaters continue to make some campuses and bus stops unsafe. In a Facebook post, the district said crews spent Monday assessing school campuses and their accessibility following widespread flooding across the county. Officials had hoped water levels would fall enough to reopen schools Tuesday, but floodwaters were still preventing safe access to some campuses Monday evening. The district also said flooding has created unsafe conditions in several areas where students would normally wait for school buses. After consulting with the Okeechobee County Emergency Operations Center, district officials said there was no guarantee conditions would improve enough overnight to safely reopen. "To avoid further delay and inconvenience to parents and the community, we have determined that keeping schools closed Tuesday is the safest decision for our students, families, and staff," the district said. District teams will continue checking conditions Tuesday and will provide additional information about when schools can reopen. Officials said the district will also announce in the coming days whether any makeup days will be necessary. The continued closure comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding across Okeechobee County, leaving neighborhoods underwater and roads difficult to navigate.

Some areas across the region received over a foot of rainfall in a day, with most of it happening in just a 12-hour period.The highest totals were just north of Sebastian, with 19.75" in Palm Bay to almost 2 feet of rain in Grant Valkaria in 24 hours. This exceeds a 1-in-1,000-year rainfall event, which is a .1% chance of this amount of rainfall happening in any given year.Radar estimates that over 20 inches of rain fell between Sunday and Monday in West Palm Beach.All of our official daily records were shattered.West Palm Beach almost tripled its previous daily record. The previous record was 2.52". This makes it the 2nd highest rainfall on a November day. The record still stands at 7.41" from November 22, 1984.TREASURE COASTVero Beach had its 2nd highest rainfall on a November day at 4.91". The record stands at 4.98" on November 4th, 1982.Fort Pierce had 5.39", nearly doubling the daily record of 2.24' from 1946. This is the third-highest total for a November day.Have we ever seen this much rain in a short period? Just a little south of us, including Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood, and Dania Beach, on April 12, 2023. Showers and thunderstorms repeatedly training over this urban corridor brought rainfall rates of 3-6 inches/hour, and 12-hour amounts exceeding 20 inches. Flash flooding left people stranded in inundated vehicles and homes, while also shutting down a major airport.

Days of relentless rain have flooded streets and homes in Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community, leaving residents struggling to salvage their belongings as the city declared a state of emergency amid continued heavy rain.WPTV's Michael Hoffman found streets deep underwater as he entered the neighborhood. Residents carried belongings in trash bags and on rafts, while one person used a kayak to make their way down a flooded street.Many residents were unable to get back into their homes as the rain continued.WATCH: Riviera Beach flooding swamps Lone Pine communityFor Luz Ortiz, the flooding was unlike anything she had experienced in more than two decades living in the community."A disaster," Ortiz said.Ortiz told Hoffman she has lived there for 21 years and never expected to see flooding like this."We didn't know it was going to happen because, since, like I said, we've been here 21 years and never happened, so we didn't expect this," Ortiz said.Another resident told Hoffman the water was already waist-high just trying to reach their home and worried that continued rainfall could make conditions even worse."That's what we're worried about. We're worried about it getting even higher than this, because just to get into my house, it's waist high," the resident said. "Just imagine it going higher than that."The City of Riviera Beach declared a state of emergency as flooding continued across the area.Other local governments across WPTV's five-county viewing area also declared states of emergency, including St. Lucie, Indian River and Martin counties.Flooding was not confined to residential neighborhoods.Hoffman also documented severe street flooding on Military Trail approaching Okeechobee Boulevard.First responders and emergency officials urged people to stay off flooded roads whenever possible and warned motorists never to drive through standing water.The guidance is simple: Turn around, don't drown.With the midterm elections approaching, flooding also forced Palm Beach County election officials to change two polling locations.The Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Office told Hoffman that voters in Precinct 6401 were reassigned from Casa Rio Clubhouse to Riviera Beach Preparatory and Achievement Academy at 7071 Garden Road in Riviera Beach.Voters in Precinct 7628 were reassigned from Ironhorse Country Club to North County Senior Center at 5217 Northlake Blvd. in Palm Beach Gardens.The changes come as residents across parts of Palm Beach County contend with flooded roads and neighborhoods following days of rain.For people in Lone Pine, the immediate concern remains what happens if the water continues to rise.Residents who spoke with Hoffman said they were already navigating waist-high water, removing belongings and trying to protect what they could as rain continued to fall.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Loved ones are mourning nine people killed when a Learjet 60 went down near Greenacres on Sunday, including a family of four, their friends and caregiver, a jet captain and a 20-year-old co-pilot from Boca Raton.The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the deadly crash as families begin sharing memories of the people whose lives were lost.“I want to express our profound condolences to the family and friends of those who were lost in this tragedy,” NTSB investigator Thomas Chapman said.Watch: Loved ones remember 9 killed in Greenacres jet crash, including Boca Raton co-pilotBoca Raton co-pilot among those killedEast Coast Jets confirmed Monday that Capt. Jeff Gregory was among those killed.The company said Gregory had previously worked for East Coast Jets briefly in 2016 and 2017 before pursuing other opportunities.“We are deeply saddened to learn that Captain Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday’s tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach,” East Coast Jets said in a statement.The co-pilot was identified as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras of Boca Raton. Her family remembered her as hardworking and responsible. WPTV also spoke off camera with Nathalia’s stepfather. As they grieve, they are not sharing a formal statement at this time.Family of four, friends and caregiver rememberedIn a joint statement, relatives identified the seven passengers aboard the Learjet as Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp; their children, 4-year-old Emma and 2-year-old Charlie; Rachael Reed; Charmi Fehr; and Anita Maria Cetina.Their relatives described Adam and Helen as devoted parents whose warmth and generosity made others feel welcome. Emma and Charlie, the family said, were “the light of their lives.”The statement also remembered Reed and Fehr for their joy, adventurous spirits and deep love for the people in their lives.Cetina cared for Emma and Charlie and had become much more than a caregiver, relatives said, describing her as part of the family and remembering the tenderness and devotion she showed the children.The families thanked first responders, investigators and the Palm Beach County community for their support. They also expressed condolences to the families of the pilots.The families have asked for privacy while they grieve and said information about memorial services will be released after arrangements are made.NTSB investigates what caused the crashAs families mourn, investigators are working to determine what led to the Learjet 60 crash.“Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again,” Chapman said.The investigation remains ongoing.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency Monday for Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties as heavy rainfall and flooding continued to affect parts of the Treasure Coast.The three Treasure Coast counties are among seven covered by Executive Order 26-227. The declaration also includes Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee and Highlands counties.The governor's office said flooding has affected and could continue to affect critical infrastructure, including state and county roads, major interstates, airports and schools. Additional heavy rain and thunderstorms were also forecast, potentially worsening flooding in already affected areas.READ THE FULL EXECUTIVE ORDER BELOW: The declaration gives state and local officials additional authority and resources to respond to the flooding. It authorizes the state coordinating officer to carry out response, recovery and mitigation efforts, including logistical, rescue and evacuation operations. The order also allows the Florida National Guard and Florida State Guard to be activated as needed.The order gives the Florida Department of Transportation authority to close roads or manage traffic when necessary and allows tolls to be waived if needed to facilitate emergency assistance or evacuations. Local governments may also waive certain procedures involving public works, contracts, equipment, workers and spending to speed up their emergency response.WATCH BELOW: Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roadsResidents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties are also covered by provisions allowing pharmacists to provide up to a 30-day emergency refill of maintenance medications. State and local facilities may be closed as necessary, and public facilities suitable for shelters must be made available if requested by local emergency management officials.The declaration also activates Florida's price-gouging protections in the affected counties for essential commodities, supplies, services and equipment needed because of the emergency.With Florida's general election scheduled for Tuesday, the order includes a provision addressing potential impacts from the flooding. Any county supervisor of elections who cannot fully comply with certain polling-place requirements must notify the Florida Department of State about proposed partial or substitute measures, which would require approval from the Florida secretary of state.The executive order took effect immediately on Monday and is scheduled to remain in effect for 60 days unless it is extended.

Neighborhoods were underwater, and schools were closed Monday following heavy rains across Okeechobee County.Justin Hazellief, public safety director and fire chief for the county, said the area experienced a 1-in-200-year rainfall event, receiving around 9 to 10 inches of rain in just six hours on Sunday.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "This is by far in my 25 years this is the worst that I've seen," Hazellief said. "Mother nature has a mind of her own, and whenever she brings that amount of rain in that short of time, there's no infrastructure anywhere that would be able to handle that amount of water and not have some consequences." The most heavily impacted area, Hazellief said, was the southwest portion of the county. Hazellief said the pumps are on and the locks are open at Taylor Creek to bring water levels down. With more rain in the forecast, Hazellief said crews are working non-stop. "They will continue to work 24/7 until we're able to restore some normalcy as far as water levels go," Hazellief said. Okeechobee County Sheriff Noel Stephen said they've been deploying their high-water rescue vehicles during the flood event. "We're just trying to ask people to slow down, take a breath, and be patient," Stephen said. Chief Donald Hagan, with Okeechobee Police, asking people to stay out of flooded areas. "If you don't live in that neighborhood, stay out of the neighborhood because you're pushing a wake that could inundate somebody's home," Hagan said. WPTV went to the Seminole Cove community, where parts of the neighborhood were completely underwater. Neighbor Debra Mauldin said she's never experienced flooding like this before. "It just kept pouring," Mauldin said. I couldn't go to work this morning, but there's nothing we can do about it." With more potential rain in the forecast, Mauldin said she's keeping her eyes to the sky. "Just hanging out, watching the rain, and hoping it doesn't get worse," Mauldin said. The Okeechobee School District said it is planning for schools to open on Tuesday.

In the neighborhood around Square Lake, Christie Oelsner surveyed the flooding from her golf cart Monday morning."This has never happened in 40 years," she said. "Last night it was up to here, waist-high."WATCH REPORT BELOW: Her home and others appeared to be spared from the flooding that filled the streets.The City of Palm Beach Gardens reports there were 15 inches of rain in 12 hours on Sunday.The city reported street flooding in places including: Sandtree PGA National Steeplechase Horseshoe Acres MontecitoThe city also made a statement about storm drains that appeared to be overwhelmed by the water."The stormwater system is performing as designed and helping mitigate the risk of flooding to homes and properties," the statement read.The city is advising drivers to avoid flooded streets and says they are making sure emergency services are also ready."Our Police, Fire Rescue, and Public Works teams have also developed contingency plans to maintain emergency response capabilities and ensure access to residents, including those in areas experiencing significant flooding."

Heavy rain is flooding roadways across the Treasure Coast, leaving drivers stranded, disrupting daily routines and prompting police to urge residents to stay off the roads unless travel is absolutely necessary.WATCH OUR COVERAGE HERE: Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie, floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas, turning roadways into lakes and covering sidewalks. Vehicles that attempted to drive through the water stalled, leaving drivers waiting for help as passing cars sent waves toward already stranded vehicles.Port St. Lucie police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters.One driver told WPTV his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children."I'm on hold with the insurance company right now trying to get some help," he said.The man, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have gotten worse following heavy rain events.Another woman found herself stranded after her vehicle stopped working just minutes after driving toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard."Every time a car comes by, it pushes my car," she told WPTV.The woman could only speak to WPTV through a small opening in her driver's side door as water continued to rush toward her vehicle. A nearby man eventually tried to help her get out.A couple nearby also described watching their vehicle sink deeper into the floodwaters after being stranded for about an hour, with waves from passing traffic pushing the car around.WATCH BELOW: Aerial video of flooding in St. Lucie WestFor some residents, the flooding created more than just a driving hazard. It also raised concerns about getting children to and from school.One woman told WPTV she was trying to figure out how to pick up her children after parents were notified they needed to retrieve their students."They just announced it, they just called parents right now to pick up kids from school. They let the kids go to school knowing it was like this," she said.She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road just last year."It was only three months old, and she got stuck here on the road because the drainage system here sucks, is so bad," she said.The woman questioned whether the city's road expansion efforts are being matched with improvements to its drainage infrastructure."They just keep widening the roads, not even worried about anything else," she said.The city says it is working on longer-term drainage improvements, including a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood.Plans include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to help address recurring flooding.However, the project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and working to clear debris from drainage systems.Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.Port St. Lucie police are asking residents to stay home and avoid traveling unless absolutely necessary.Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and remind drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

Hundreds of people forced from their homes after a deadly Learjet crash near Greenacres are now facing a difficult reality: they don't know when they'll be allowed back.An estimated 400 to 600 people were displaced as investigators secured the surrounding mobile home neighborhood and began combing through debris scattered throughout their houses.WATCH REPORT BELOW: WPTV is listening to residents impacted and met Armando Perez.He says his mobile home is just about 250 feet from where the crash happened. But right now, he can't get to his house, his vehicle or the tools he needs to work."I have a regular life like everybody does, and all of us just want a little bit of our lives back, I guess," Perez said.Perez was home when the Learjet crashed and remembers feeling the impact before he fully understood what was happening."If you could visualize, if you could feel noise, then that's how I felt. I felt the noise in my body," Perez said. "I felt the pressure that sent through my walls when I was sleeping."Within minutes, neighbors were coming out of their homes, trying to figure out what had happened.Eventually, residents learned a jet had gone down nearby. Then came the evacuation.Perez said residents were given time to grab the necessities for a couple of days. He took clothes, his passport, a toothbrush and other hygiene products. His vehicle, however, stayed behind, along with the tools and equipment he uses to make a living."Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez said.Perez works as a handyman, making access to those tools and his vehicle especially important. He said the longer he remains displaced, the more worried he becomes about the financial impact."Please help us as soon as possible, please, and help us with what is really needed," Perez said. "We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made."Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said residents have not been allowed back because the area is still being investigated."They're combing through all the evidence. Once that is clear, they'll gain access," Flores said. "We're hoping to try to see if there's a way that we can get their vehicles out once that crime scene is gone through, but at this point in time we don't really know when."Flores said that the crash happened near the entrance of the mobile park and said there's no way to go in or out without interfering with the scene."You know, it could be up to two weeks. We don't really know," Flores said. "I'm trying to get people to at least get their vehicles."Around 50 people stayed overnight at the Greenacres Community Center, according to Flores. The county initially opened two shelter sites but later consolidated them into one.Perez was among those who stayed at the community center."It wasn't bad, Joel. They did the best they can for us, and they have, and I hope they still do," Perez said.While WPTV was on scene, emergency officials brought mobile showers to the shelter and is working on other forms of assistance. Flores said he's trying to secure hotel vouchers as well as food and Palm Tran vouchers for people who do not have access to their vehicles.The problems extend beyond the investigation itself.Flores said a water main broke, causing a water outage in the neighborhood and nearby businesses. Crews need to pump water out before reaching some of the debris, and rain has made that work more difficult."Because of the water main breaking, we have to pump all the water out so that we're able to get to the debris, and with the rain last night and we're expecting more rain, it's making the process go a lot slower," Flores said.Florida state Rep. Debra Tendrich said debris from the aircraft has been scattered throughout the surrounding community, stretching roughly two miles."Some of those pieces are very sharp," Tendrich said. "And so in order for us to make sure our community is safe, we also want people to look out in their backyards and around their homes to make sure that when they're out with their kids or walking their dogs that they're not stepping on these items."Residents who find potential evidence or witnessed the crash can report it by calling 561-688-3375, Tendrich said.She's also looking ahead to another problem residents could face when they're finally allowed home: food.With power shut off in the affected area, Tendrich said some families may return to refrigerators filled with food that has to be thrown away."What's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement, she said that's another expense she doesn't want them to have to shoulder alone."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family, and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.For Perez, getting back home also means getting back some sense of normalcy. While he understands investigators still have a job to do, he said the uncertainty is taking a toll financially and mentally."I understand that there's lives and things that happened, but I'm alive too," Perez said. "Our lives are tied up in an investigation."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Both Okeechobee County and Martin County Public Schools will be closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, as flooding and severe weather continue to create unsafe travel conditions across the region.MARTIN COUNTY SCHOOLS CLOSED All Martin County School District-operated schools will be closed Tuesday, which will also include all after-school activities.School officials said in a Facebook post that conditions vary significantly across the region, with some communities experiencing serious flooding and difficult travel conditions.The district said many of its employees and families live outside Martin County and commute into the county each day. Those conditions in neighboring communities played an important role in the decision to close schools.Throughout Monday, the district received reports of employees and families driving through floodwaters to get home, abandoning vehicles because of impassable roads and making alternate overnight accommodations because they could not safely remain in their homes.Officials said they also considered whether employees would be able to safely travel to and from campuses and whether schools would have enough staff and resources to safely support students throughout the day.The district said the decision follows Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' declaration of a state of emergency covering Martin County and surrounding counties."We encourage everyone to use caution and prioritize their safety as conditions continue to affect our region," the district said.Families are being asked to monitor the Martin County School District's website and social media accounts for additional updates.OKEECHOBEE COUNTY SCHOOLS CLOSEDOkeechobee County district officials announced Monday evening that lingering floodwaters continue to make some campuses and bus stops unsafe.In a Facebook post, the district said crews spent Monday assessing school campuses and their accessibility following widespread flooding across the county.Officials had hoped water levels would fall enough to reopen schools Tuesday, but floodwaters were still preventing safe access to some campuses Monday evening.The district also said flooding has created unsafe conditions in several areas where students would normally wait for school buses.After consulting with the Okeechobee County Emergency Operations Center, district officials said there was no guarantee conditions would improve enough overnight to safely reopen."To avoid further delay and inconvenience to parents and the community, we have determined that keeping schools closed Tuesday is the safest decision for our students, families, and staff," the district said.District teams will continue checking conditions Tuesday and will provide additional information about when schools can reopen.Officials said the district will also announce in the coming days whether any makeup days will be necessary.The continued closure comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding across Okeechobee County, leaving neighborhoods underwater and roads difficult to navigate.

Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency Monday for Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties as heavy rainfall and flooding continued to affect parts of the Treasure Coast.The three Treasure Coast counties are among seven covered by Executive Order 26-227. The declaration also includes Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee and Highlands counties.The governor's office said flooding has affected and could continue to affect critical infrastructure, including state and county roads, major interstates, airports and schools. Additional heavy rain and thunderstorms were also forecast, potentially worsening flooding in already affected areas.READ THE FULL EXECUTIVE ORDER BELOW: The declaration gives state and local officials additional authority and resources to respond to the flooding. It authorizes the state coordinating officer to carry out response, recovery and mitigation efforts, including logistical, rescue and evacuation operations. The order also allows the Florida National Guard and Florida State Guard to be activated as needed.The order gives the Florida Department of Transportation authority to close roads or manage traffic when necessary and allows tolls to be waived if needed to facilitate emergency assistance or evacuations. Local governments may also waive certain procedures involving public works, contracts, equipment, workers and spending to speed up their emergency response.WATCH BELOW: Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roadsResidents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties are also covered by provisions allowing pharmacists to provide up to a 30-day emergency refill of maintenance medications. State and local facilities may be closed as necessary, and public facilities suitable for shelters must be made available if requested by local emergency management officials.The declaration also activates Florida's price-gouging protections in the affected counties for essential commodities, supplies, services and equipment needed because of the emergency.With Florida's general election scheduled for Tuesday, the order includes a provision addressing potential impacts from the flooding. Any county supervisor of elections who cannot fully comply with certain polling-place requirements must notify the Florida Department of State about proposed partial or substitute measures, which would require approval from the Florida secretary of state.The executive order took effect immediately on Monday and is scheduled to remain in effect for 60 days unless it is extended.

They let the kids go to school knowing it was like this," she said.She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road just last year."It was only three months old, and she got stuck here on the road because the drainage system here sucks, is so bad," she said.The woman questioned whether the city's road expansion efforts are being matched with improvements to its drainage infrastructure."They just keep widening the roads, not even worried about anything else," she said.The city says it is working on longer-term drainage improvements, including a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood.Plans include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to help address recurring flooding.However, the project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and working to clear debris from drainage systems.Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.Port St. Lucie police are asking residents to stay home and avoid traveling unless absolutely necessary.Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and remind drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

Lucie County has declared a local state of emergency due to heavy rain causing widespread flooding across the area. The county’s emergency operations center is partially activated to coordinate response efforts and manage resources. Hearst Owned WPBF 25 News St. Lucie County has issued a local state of emergency as heavy rain causes flooding, with officials urging residents to avoid travel and activating emergency response efforts. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Officials are urging residents to stay off the roads this evening, if possible, to ensure safety. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. You can download it here .

Lucie voters assigned to Precinct 90 at Legacy High School can vote there Tuesday, despite flooding and road closures that are making it difficult to reach the polling location, the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections office confirmed to CBS12 News. The elections office is directing voters to take Midway Road and Glade Extension to get to the school. CBS12 News had a crew on the scene who said they encountered flooding and roadblocks on Southwest Village Parkway earlier Tuesday and had to turn around. Police had blocked that entrance, but voters could reach Legacy High School by taking an alternate route. The flooding and changing information about the polling location caused confusion for some voters. CBS12 News Paige Meyer reported that voters were being directed to Tradition Town Hall, though it could take a couple of hours to get the site ready. See also: Florida Amendment 3: What a yes or no vote means for homeowners and local services Voter Tommy Sharpe said he was directed there but was told he could not vote because it was not his assigned precinct. He said he was then told Legacy was open and he would need to take a back route. Sharpe said the detour to Legacy would add 20 to 35 minutes to his drive. Voters who cannot reach Legacy High School can go to the Tradition office at 10-267 Southwest Village Parkway, where election staff can print a vote-by-mail ballot. Voters can complete and sign the ballot and return it as directed by staff, the elections office said. Lucie voters are choosing the city’s next mayor Tuesday. Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students one hour early Monday and cancel all after-school activities as heavy rainfall and flooding continue to impact the county. The district announced that all students will be dismissed one hour earlier than their regularly scheduled dismissal times. All after-school activities, including aftercare programs, have also been canceled. The changes come after parts of St. Lucie County received up to 6 inches of rain. Earlier Monday, the district announced that parents and guardians could pick up their children early, with one exception. Oak Hammock K-8 School is not allowing early pickups because of flooding in front of the school, according to the district. It was not immediately clear how the flooding would affect the school's updated dismissal schedule. See also: Boca Raton co-pilot, 20, killed in fiery Florida jet crash, family confirms The district says all student absences Monday will be excused. Families are urged to plan for adjusted dismissal times and monitor the district's website and social media channels for updates.

Lucie police are urging drivers to avoid portions of St. Lucie West as significant water accumulation creates hazardous conditions on area roadways.The Port St. Lucie Police Department said in a post on its Facebook page that several roads have become difficult to navigate because of high water and asked motorists to stay out of the area unless travel is absolutely necessary.Police said officers are responding to reports of vehicles stranded in high-water conditions.Drivers are being warned not to attempt to travel through standing water. Police are advising motorists who encounter flooding to turn around and find an alternate route."Never underestimate the depth or power of floodwaters," the department said in its news release.Police said officers are continuing to monitor conditions and will provide updates as road closures and other traffic impacts develop.Residents are also being asked to stay off the roads if possible and give emergency responders room to work.The flooding comes amid heavy rain affecting the Treasure Coast, with areas receiving repeated rounds of downpours.

As the flooding response shifts to cleanup and recovery, the Port St. Lucie Police Department is working with local towing companies to remove disabled and abandoned vehicles obstructing roadways. The vehicles can pose safety hazards, impede traffic and prevent crews from safely reaching affected areas, the department said in a Facebook post Tuesday. Vehicles removed during the operation are being taken to the MidFlorida Event Center , located at 9221 SE Event Center Place. The site is serving as a temporary vehicle storage and recovery location. Owners can go to the event center to retrieve a vehicle towed as part of the operation. Personnel will verify ownership before releasing it. See also: Flooding prompts St. Lucie County closures, could affect Election Day voting The towing companies assisting with the effort are ABC Towing , Towmasters PSL, Tow Boys Inc. , All Hooked Up and Kauffs Towing. Lucie Police Department thanked residents for their patience and cooperation as crews continue clearing roads and assisting the community’s recovery.

Several neighborhoods in Vero Beach were flooded Monday after rounds of heavy rain moved through the area. The scene along 41st Avenue and 12th Street, about a mile from Glendale Elementary School, showed water covering roads, front lawns and driveways. Neighbors said they have never seen flooding this severe in the area before. Residents say the steady rain throughout the day overwhelmed drainage systems, leaving water with nowhere to go but into neighborhood streets and yards. A photo shared by the sheriff's office showed just how high the water rose at one point, with only the roof of an SUV visible above the floodwaters. Authorities have not said whether anyone was inside the vehicle. See also: See updated polling locations due to severe weather across South Florida Deputies are urging residents to stay off the roads and avoid driving through flooded areas, warning that conditions remain unsafe. A CBS12 News crew will be back in affected neighborhoods Tuesday morning to assess any damage as residents continue waiting for floodwaters to recede.

The Indian River County Government announced on Monday, Nov. 2, that the county is under a local state of emergency because of flooding. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Indian River County Administrator John A. said the local state of emergency was enacted because of deteriorating weather conditions, the impassability of numerous roadways due to flooding and continuing rainfall in all areas of Indian River County. The state of emergency became active at 2:30 p.m. Monday and will last until further notice. VOLUNTARY EVACUATION The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Monday night that a voluntary evacuation order is in effect for the Rockridge neighborhood (17th Street to 13th Place, 6th Avenue to IR BLVD) due to flooding and potential wastewater backups. Indian River County Utilities is monitoring conditions and has contacted affected customers. The sheriff's office said if residents had questions or wanted to report their status, they should call 772-226-4000. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County opening flood shelters in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is opening temporary shelters at Northport K-8 School in Port St. Lucie and the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce for residents whose homes were flooded. The shelters follow excessive flooding in the county Nov. 2.

Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive, is scheduled to open Nov. 3 at 11 a.m. The Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave, is designated as a special needs shelter and is scheduled to open Nov. 3 at 1 p.m.

Residents should bring pillows, blankets, non-perishable food and one gallon of water per person per day. They should also bring important papers, medications, glasses and additional clothing.

cards.headline: Flooded Port St. Lucie roads remain hazardous as crews check Creekside homes
cards.teaser: SW Rosser Road at SW Paar Drive and SW Delos Drive remained flooded and impassable Tuesday morning. Emergency crews were checking homes in Creekside as police monitored roads across Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
Flooded roads remained hazardous across Port St. Lucie on Tuesday morning, with SW Rosser Road at SW Paar Drive and SW Delos Drive still impassable as water receded elsewhere. The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office drone team was working with the St. Lucie County Fire District to conduct home checks in the Creekside community.

Police reported flooding or barricades at Port St. Lucie Boulevard at Aviation Avenue; northbound Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Dalton Boulevard to Gatlin Boulevard; Selvitz Road from Midway Road to Peachtree Boulevard; and Peachtree Boulevard. Other affected locations included Westmoreland Boulevard in front of The Anchorage, Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, St. Lucie West Boulevard, Volusia Drive from Blanton Boulevard to Torino Parkway, California Boulevard in front of Fire Station 14, Country Club Estates of St. Lucie West and northbound Cashmere Boulevard.

Aerial footage shared by police showed significant flooding near SW Savage Boulevard, SW Fairgreen Road and SW Salvatierra Boulevard, with water spread across residential streets and surrounding areas. Flooding also affected roads and neighborhoods near Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard, as well as Torino Parkway, NW California Boulevard and NW Peacock Boulevard. Police said standing water made travel hazardous in those areas.

Water was beginning to recede on Lennard Road at Melaleuca Boulevard, Hillmoor Drive in front of HCA St. Lucie Medical Center and near the 1700 block, and Village Green Drive. Vehicles could pass on those roads, police said, though four disabled vehicles on Lennard Road awaited removal.

Flooding had subsided on Becker Road from Hallmark Street to Savona Boulevard, Darwin Boulevard and College Park Road. Several disabled vehicles remained on Becker and Darwin. Water had also cleared on Darwin Boulevard at Fifer Avenue, where two disabled vehicles remained. Rosser Boulevard had cleared, while the intersections on SW Rosser Road remained flooded and impassable.

Police extended patrol shifts overnight to keep additional officers available for emergencies. Officers assessed roads and neighborhoods at daybreak, helped stranded motorists, responded to calls and monitored flooding throughout the city.

Police urged residents to stay home unless travel was necessary, avoid flooded roads and never drive through standing water. The department cautioned that conditions could change quickly, especially with more rain. Residents should call 911 to report downed power lines, fallen trees, road obstructions or other hazards posing an immediate danger.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie clears flood-disabled vehicles from roads, offers pickup at event center
cards.teaser: Vehicles towed during the cleanup operation are being taken to the MidFlorida Event Center. Owners can retrieve them after personnel verify ownership.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department is working with local towing companies to remove disabled and abandoned vehicles blocking roads as the flooding response shifts to cleanup and recovery. Vehicles removed during the operation are being taken to the MidFlorida Event Center at 9221 SE Event Center Place, where owners can retrieve them after personnel verify ownership.

The event center is serving as a temporary vehicle storage and recovery location. In a Facebook post Tuesday, the department said vehicles obstructing roadways can pose safety hazards, impede traffic and prevent crews from safely reaching affected areas.

ABC Towing, Towmasters PSL, Tow Boys Inc., All Hooked Up and Kauffs Towing are assisting with the operation. The department thanked residents for their patience and cooperation as crews continue clearing roads and assisting the community’s recovery.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie tests flood sensors as Oak Hammock drainage project could take years
cards.teaser: The city says Oak Hammock drainage improvements remain in data collection. Crews are testing water-level sensors and clearing drainage debris as flooded roads strand drivers.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie is testing water-level sensors and clearing drainage debris as heavy rain floods roads and strands drivers, while a drainage project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood remains in the data-collection phase. The city says the project, which includes new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raised portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard, could take years to complete.

The planned Oak Hammock improvements are intended to address recurring flooding. In the meantime, the city says it is testing sensors to help crews respond more quickly to rising water. Crews are also clearing debris from drainage systems, checking water flow and addressing potholes reported to the city or discovered during inspections.

Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas and covered sidewalks. Vehicles stalled as drivers attempted to cross the water, leaving them waiting for help while passing traffic sent waves toward their cars. Port St. Lucie police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters. One driver’s vehicle stopped working while he was trying to pick up his children. A nearby couple described being stranded for about an hour as their vehicle sank deeper into the water and waves from passing traffic pushed it around.

Flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman said parents had been notified to retrieve their children, leaving her trying to figure out how to reach them. She said her sister’s nearly new vehicle was lost to flooding on the same road last year, when it was only three months old. The woman questioned whether the city’s road expansion efforts were being matched by drainage improvements. Another driver, who said he had lived in the area for six years, said he believed drainage conditions had worsened after heavy rain.

Port St. Lucie police are urging residents to stay home and avoid travel unless absolutely necessary. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and remind drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

cards.headline: Legacy High School polling site remains open amid Port St. Lucie flooding
cards.teaser: Precinct 90 voters should take Midway Road and Glade Extension to reach the school. Voters unable to get there can obtain a vote-by-mail ballot at the elections office’s Tradition office.
cards.body:
Precinct 90 at Legacy High School in Port St. Lucie remains open for voting Tuesday despite flooding and road closures that have made the polling location difficult to reach, the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections office confirmed. The office is directing voters to take Midway Road and Glade Extension to the school. Flooding and roadblocks affected Southwest Village Parkway earlier Tuesday, and police blocked that entrance. Voters could still reach the school by the alternate route. Port St. Lucie voters are choosing the city’s next mayor Tuesday.

Voters who cannot reach Legacy High School can go to the elections office’s Tradition office at 10-267 Southwest Village Parkway, where election staff can print a vote-by-mail ballot. Voters can complete and sign the ballot, then return it as directed by staff, the elections office said. That option is separate from voting at Tradition Town Hall, which is the assigned polling location for Precinct 92.

Flooding and changing information about the polling location caused confusion for some voters. Tommy Sharpe said he was directed to Tradition Town Hall but was told he could not vote there because it was not his assigned precinct. He said he was then told Legacy High School was open and he would need to take a back route. Sharpe said the detour would add 20 to 35 minutes to his drive. Tradition Town Hall is at 10799 SW Civic Lane and replaced The Brennity at Tradition as Precinct 92’s polling location.

Other St. Lucie County polling locations include the Port St. Lucie Community Center, 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., for precincts 49, 51 and 71, with access from Airoso Boulevard. Precincts 49 and 71 previously voted at Oak Hammock K-8 School, while Precinct 51 previously used Disabled American Veterans Hall. Precincts 85 and 95 are assigned to the MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place, replacing Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence. Precinct 12 is at Days Inn Midtown, 3224 S. Highway 1 in Fort Pierce, replacing Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge. Precincts 6 and 28 are at Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce, replacing Renaissance Business Park, formerly Orange Blossom Business Center. Paula A. Lewis Library also remains open as a polling location.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County, Port St. Lucie declare flood emergencies as county activates response center
hero.body:
St. Lucie County and the City of Port St. Lucie declared local states of emergency Monday as flooding affected streets and neighborhoods. The county’s Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation, with Public Safety personnel coordinating the response with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments. County officials said the declaration would expedite access to additional resources that may be needed.

Crews are working to address flooding problems across St. Lucie County. Officials urged residents to refrain from traveling Monday evening if possible and warned motorists against driving through flooded roads. Port St. Lucie issued its emergency declaration in alignment with the county. The City Council was scheduled to meet Tuesday at 1 p.m. at City Hall to vote to formally approve the State of Emergency, which can help expedite additional resources as needed.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County warned residents about health hazards associated with floodwaters. Health officials advise people to avoid contact with floodwater, particularly if they have open cuts or sores, and not to eat or drink anything contaminated by it. Anyone whose wounds have been exposed to floodwater should thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Heavy rainfall could also make water from flooded private wells unsafe to drink, health officials said. Residents who are unsure whether flooding has affected their wells should use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing their teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. People whose septic systems are experiencing slow plumbing should conserve water and avoid having their septic tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high.

Indian River County also declared a local state of emergency Monday, citing ongoing flooding, deteriorating weather and continued rainfall. County officials said numerous roads had become impassable. The county urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel through flood-affected areas, obey road closures and barricades, and never drive through flooded roadways. Both counties asked residents to continue monitoring official sources as conditions change.

cards.headline: Knee-deep flooding strands drivers on Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Police urge residents to avoid unnecessary travel as floodwaters stall vehicles. The city's Oak Hammock drainage project remains in data collection and could take years to complete.
cards.body:
Heavy rain left drivers stranded on Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie, where floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas and covered sidewalks. Vehicles stalled as drivers tried to cross the water, and passing traffic sent waves toward stranded cars. Port St. Lucie police said officers were responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters and urged residents to avoid travel unless absolutely necessary.

One driver said his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children, leaving him waiting for help from his insurance company. The man, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have worsened following heavy rain. Another woman's vehicle stopped working minutes after she drove toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. Water rushed toward her vehicle, and a nearby man tried to help her get out. A couple stranded for about an hour described watching their vehicle sink deeper as waves from passing traffic pushed it around.

The flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman said parents had been notified to retrieve their children, leaving her trying to figure out how to reach them. She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year. The vehicle was only three months old, she said. The woman questioned whether the city's road-widening work was being matched by drainage improvements.

The city says it is working on longer-term drainage improvements, including a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood. Plans call for new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to address recurring flooding. The project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.

In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.

Police are asking residents to stay home unless travel is absolutely necessary. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

hero.headline: Flooding covers Vero Beach neighborhood roads as deputies warn drivers to stay away
hero.body:
Heavy rain flooded roads, front lawns and driveways in several Vero Beach neighborhoods Monday, prompting deputies to urge residents to stay off roads and avoid driving through floodwaters. Deputies warned that conditions remained unsafe after rounds of rain moved through the area.

Water covered streets and properties along 41st Avenue and 12th Street, about a mile from Glendale Elementary School. Neighbors said they had never seen flooding this severe in the area. Residents said steady rain throughout the day overwhelmed drainage systems, sending water into neighborhood streets and yards.

A photo shared by the sheriff's office showed only the roof of an SUV above the floodwaters at one point. Residents continued waiting for the water to recede.

A photo shared by the sheriff's office showed just how high the water rose at one point, with only the roof of an SUV visible above the floodwaters. hero.headline: Flooding forces Election Day polling relocations across St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Flooding and unsafe road conditions have forced temporary polling place relocations across St. Lucie County for Tuesday’s election. Election officials are urging voters to verify their assigned locations before leaving home because additional changes may be necessary as flooding conditions evolve.

Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced the changes Monday, saying the relocations are intended to give voters safe and accessible places to cast their ballots. Voters can check for updates at www.stlucievotes.gov or contact the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500.

The polling location changes are:

• Precinct 12, Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge: Voting moves to Days Inn Midtown (Precinct 25), 3224 S. 1, Fort Pierce, FL 34982.

• Precincts 49 and 71, Oak Hammock K-8 School: Voting moves to Port St. Lucie Community Center (Precinct 45), 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Precinct 51, Disabled American Veterans Hall: Voting moves to Port St. Lucie Community Center (Precinct 45), 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Lucie West Centennial High School: Voting moves to Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence, 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34986. Access is from Peacock Boulevard.

• Lewis Library: Voting moves to Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

• Precinct 92, The Brennity at Tradition: Voting moves to Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

The relocations follow days of heavy rainfall. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and infrastructure.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways.
