cards.headline: St. Lucie County declares flooding emergency; Port St. Lucie schedules Tuesday vote
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County's Emergency Operations Center is under a Level 2 partial activation. Health officials are warning residents about floodwater exposure and potentially unsafe private-well water.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County declared a local state of emergency Monday afternoon as flooding affected streets and neighborhoods, a step intended to expedite access to additional resources. The City of Port St. Lucie also declared an emergency, with the City Council scheduled to vote Tuesday at 1 p.m. at City Hall to formally approve it.

The county's Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation. Public Safety personnel are coordinating with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments in response to the flooding. Crews are working to address problems across the county. Officials urged residents to avoid travel Monday evening if possible and warned motorists against attempting to drive through flooded roads. Port St. Lucie's declaration aligns with the county's and can help expedite additional resources as needed.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County is warning residents about potential health hazards associated with floodwaters. Residents should avoid eating or drinking anything contaminated with floodwater and avoid contact with floodwater, particularly if they have open cuts or sores. Anyone whose wounds have been exposed should thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Health officials also warned that heavy rainfall could make water from flooded private wells unsafe to drink. Residents unsure whether flooding has affected their well should use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing their teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. People with septic systems experiencing slow plumbing should conserve water and avoid having their septic tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high. County officials are asking residents to continue monitoring official sources as conditions change.

cards.headline: Flooding strands Port St. Lucie drivers as Oak Hammock drainage project could take years
cards.teaser: Floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep along parts of Southwest Airoso Boulevard. The city says it is testing water-level sensors and clearing drainage systems while planning longer-term improvements.
cards.body:
Heavy rain stranded drivers in Port St. Lucie as floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep along parts of Southwest Airoso Boulevard, while a city drainage project aimed at recurring flooding in Oak Hammock remains in the data-collection phase. The city says that project could take years to complete. Police are responding to a significant number of calls involving stranded vehicles and urging residents to avoid travel unless absolutely necessary.

Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, water covered sidewalks and stalled vehicles whose drivers attempted to cross flooded stretches. Passing cars sent waves toward vehicles already stuck. One man said his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children. “I'm on hold with the insurance company right now trying to get some help,” he said. The man, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have worsened following heavy rain events.

Another driver became stranded after her vehicle stopped working just minutes after she drove toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. “Every time a car comes by, it pushes my car,” she said. Water continued rushing toward her vehicle, and a nearby man eventually tried to help her get out. A couple nearby described watching their vehicle sink deeper into the floodwaters after being stranded for about an hour, with passing traffic pushing waves against the car.

The flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman said she was trying to figure out how to retrieve her children after parents were notified to pick up their students. She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year and questioned whether the city's road widening efforts were being matched with drainage improvements.

The city's Oak Hammock plans include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to help address recurring flooding. In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.

Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

hero.headline: Martin County district schools closed Tuesday, after-school activities canceled
hero.body:
All Martin County School District-operated schools will be closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, and all after-school activities are canceled as flooding and severe weather create unsafe travel conditions. District officials said the decision took into account the safety of students, families and employees, including those who commute into Martin County from neighboring communities.

Conditions vary significantly across the region, with some communities experiencing serious flooding and difficult travel, school officials said in a Facebook post. Throughout Monday, the district received reports of employees and families driving through floodwaters to get home, abandoning vehicles because roads were impassable and making alternate overnight accommodations because they could not safely remain in their homes. The district said many employees and families live outside Martin County, and conditions in those neighboring communities played an important role in the closure decision.

Officials also considered whether employees could safely travel to and from campuses and whether schools would have enough staff and resources to support students safely throughout the day. The district said the closure follows Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' declaration of a state of emergency covering Martin County and surrounding counties. “We encourage everyone to use caution and prioritize their safety as conditions continue to affect our region,” the district said. Families are asked to monitor the Martin County School District's website and social media accounts for updates.

Okeechobee County schools also will remain closed Tuesday. District officials announced Monday evening that lingering floodwaters continued to prevent safe access to some campuses and had created unsafe conditions at several school bus waiting areas. Crews assessed campuses and access routes Monday, and officials consulted with the Okeechobee County Emergency Operations Center before deciding to keep schools closed. District teams will continue checking conditions Tuesday and provide updates about reopening. Officials also plan to announce in the coming days whether makeup days will be necessary.

hero.headline: Flooding strands Port St. Lucie drivers as police urge residents to stay off roads
hero.body:
Heavy rain has stranded drivers on flooded Port St. Lucie roads, prompting police to urge residents to stay home unless travel is absolutely necessary. Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, water reached approximately knee-deep in some areas, covered sidewalks and stalled vehicles. Police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving stranded vehicles. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

Drivers caught in the flooding waited for help as passing traffic sent waves toward their vehicles. One man said his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children, leaving him seeking help from his insurance company. Another driver became stranded minutes after heading toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. Water rushed toward her vehicle, and passing cars pushed it around. A nearby man eventually tried to help her get out. A couple also described watching their vehicle sink deeper into floodwaters after they had been stranded for about an hour.

The flooding also complicated school pickups and renewed residents’ concerns about drainage. One woman said she was trying to figure out how to retrieve her children after parents were notified to pick up their students. She said her sister had lost a vehicle that was only three months old to flooding on the same road last year. The woman questioned whether the city’s road widening efforts were being matched by drainage improvements. The man seeking insurance help said he had lived in the area for six years and believed drainage conditions had worsened following heavy rain.

The city says longer-term drainage improvements include a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood, with plans for new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raised portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard. That project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete. In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond faster to flooding and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or found during inspections.

hero.headline: Flooding forces Election Day polling place relocations in St. Lucie County

Election officials are urging voters to verify their assigned polling places before leaving home, as additional changes may be necessary as flooding conditions evolve.

The polling place changes are:

• Precinct 12, Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge: Voting has moved to Days Inn Midtown (Precinct 25), 3224 S. 1, Fort Pierce, FL 34982.

• Precincts 49 and 71, Oak Hammock K-8 School: Voting has moved to Port St. Lucie Community Center (Precinct 45), 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Precinct 51, Disabled American Veterans Hall: Voting has moved to Port St. Lucie Community Center (Precinct 45), 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Lucie West Centennial High School: Voting has moved to Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence, 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34986. Access is from Peacock Boulevard.

• Lewis Library: Voting has moved to Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

• Precinct 92, The Brennity at Tradition: Voting has moved to Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

The relocations follow heavy rainfall and widespread flooding. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of flooding and threats to public safety and infrastructure.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie tests water-level sensors as flooding strands drivers
cards.teaser: Crews are clearing drainage systems while the Oak Hammock improvement project remains in data collection and could take years to complete.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie is testing water-level sensors and clearing debris from drainage systems as heavy rain floods roads and strands drivers. A longer-term drainage project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete, according to the city.

Plans for Oak Hammock include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to address recurring flooding. The city says the sensors being tested would help crews respond more quickly to flooding. Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.

Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas and covered sidewalks. Vehicles stalled as drivers attempted to pass through the water, leaving them waiting for help while passing traffic sent waves toward their vehicles. Port St. Lucie police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters.

One driver said his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children. He had lived in the area for six years and believed drainage conditions had worsened following heavy rain events. Another woman became stranded after her vehicle stopped working minutes after she drove toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. A nearby man eventually tried to help her get out. A couple described watching their vehicle sink deeper into floodwaters after they had been stranded for about an hour.

The flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman said she was trying to figure out how to retrieve her children after parents were notified to pick up students. She said her sister had lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year and questioned whether the city's road widening was being matched with drainage improvements.

Port St. Lucie police are asking residents to stay home and avoid travel unless absolutely necessary. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

hero.headline: Martin County district schools to close Tuesday as flooding makes travel unsafe
hero.body:
All Martin County School District-operated schools will be closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, and all after-school activities are canceled as flooding creates unsafe travel conditions for families and staff. District officials said serious flooding in some communities, including neighboring areas where employees and families live, played an important role in the decision.

Throughout Monday, the district received reports of employees and families driving through floodwaters to get home and abandoning vehicles because roads were impassable. Others made alternate overnight accommodations because they could not safely remain in their homes. In a Facebook post, school officials said conditions vary significantly across the region, with some communities facing serious flooding and difficult travel.

Many district employees and families live outside Martin County and commute into the county each day. Officials said they considered whether employees could safely travel to and from campuses, as well as whether schools would have enough staff and resources to safely support students throughout the day.

The district said the closure follows Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' declaration of a state of emergency covering Martin County and surrounding counties. “We encourage everyone to use caution and prioritize their safety as conditions continue to affect our region,” the district said. Families are being asked to monitor the Martin County School District's website and social media accounts for additional updates.

Okeechobee County schools will also remain closed Tuesday. District officials announced Monday evening that lingering floodwaters continued to make some campuses and bus stops unsafe. Crews spent Monday assessing campuses and access after widespread flooding. Officials had hoped water levels would fall enough to reopen Tuesday, but floodwaters were still preventing safe access to some campuses Monday evening.

Okeechobee County district officials consulted with the Okeechobee County Emergency Operations Center before deciding to keep schools closed. District teams will continue checking conditions Tuesday and provide updates about reopening. Officials also said the district will announce in the coming days whether makeup days will be necessary.

hero.headline: DeSantis declares flooding emergency for all three Treasure Coast counties
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency Monday for Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties as heavy rainfall and flooding continued across parts of the Treasure Coast, with additional heavy rain and thunderstorms forecast. The governor's office said flooding has affected and could continue to affect critical infrastructure, including state and county roads, major interstates, airports and schools. The forecast rain could worsen flooding in already affected areas. Executive Order 26-227 covers seven counties, including Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee and Highlands.

The declaration gives state and local officials additional authority and resources for flood response. It authorizes the state coordinating officer to carry out response, recovery and mitigation efforts, including logistical, rescue and evacuation operations. The Florida National Guard and Florida State Guard may be activated as needed. The Florida Department of Transportation can close roads or manage traffic when necessary, and tolls may be waived to facilitate emergency assistance or evacuations. Local governments may waive certain procedures involving public works, contracts, equipment, workers and spending to speed up their emergency response.

Residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties are covered by provisions allowing pharmacists to provide up to a 30-day emergency refill of maintenance medications. The declaration also activates Florida's price-gouging protections in the affected counties for essential commodities, supplies, services and equipment needed because of the emergency. State and local facilities may be closed as necessary. Public facilities suitable for shelters must be made available if local emergency management officials request them.

With Florida's general election scheduled for Tuesday, the order also addresses potential flooding impacts on polling places. Any county supervisor of elections who cannot fully comply with certain polling-place requirements must notify the Florida Department of State about proposed partial or substitute measures. Those measures would require approval from the Florida secretary of state. The executive order took effect immediately Monday and is scheduled to remain in effect for 60 days unless extended.

cards.headline: Two shelters open in Indian River County amid widespread flooding
cards.teaser: Indian River County said shelters were open Monday night in Sebastian and Vero Beach, with the Vero Beach location accepting pets. Emergency declarations are in effect as flooding affects roads and neighborhoods.
cards.body:
Indian River County said two shelters were open Monday night, including a pet-friendly location in Vero Beach, as heavy rainfall flooded roads and neighborhoods across the Treasure Coast. Indian River County, St. Lucie County and the City of Port St. Lucie declared local states of emergency in response to the flooding.

The shelters are at Sebastian River Middle School, located at 9400 Co Rd 512 in Sebastian, and Osceola Magnet School (formerly Osceola Middle School), located at 480 20th Ave SW, Vero Beach. The Osceola Magnet School location is pet-friendly. Residents can report non-emergency flooding or property damage through the online reporting portal at IndianRiver.gov. For information or questions, the county provided 772-226-4000.

Indian River County’s emergency order took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday and remains in effect until further order. County officials said numerous roads had become impassable and that the declaration authorizes emergency actions, coordination of response efforts and measures to address hazardous conditions. The county urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel through flood-affected areas, obey road closures and barricades, and never drive through flooded roadways.

St. Lucie County’s Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation. Public Safety personnel are coordinating with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments while crews address flooding across the county. Officials asked residents to avoid travel Monday evening if possible. The City of Port St. Lucie declared its emergency in alignment with the county. The City Council is scheduled to meet Tuesday at 1 p.m. at City Hall to vote on formal approval.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County warned residents to avoid contact with floodwater, particularly with open cuts or sores, and to avoid eating or drinking anything contaminated by it. Anyone whose wounds contact floodwater should thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Health officials advised residents unsure whether flooding affected their private wells to use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. People with septic systems experiencing slow plumbing should conserve water and avoid having their tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high. Both counties asked residents to monitor official communications as conditions change.

cards.headline: Flooding strands drivers in Port St. Lucie as police urge residents to stay home
cards.teaser: Water reached approximately knee-deep along parts of Southwest Airoso Boulevard, where vehicles stalled and passing traffic pushed waves toward stranded cars. A city drainage project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.
cards.body:
Heavy rain flooded Port St. Lucie roads and stranded drivers, prompting police to urge residents to stay home unless travel is absolutely necessary. Officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters, according to Port St. Lucie police.

Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, water reached approximately knee-deep in some areas and covered sidewalks. Vehicles stalled as drivers attempted to cross the flooded roadway, leaving them waiting for help while passing traffic sent waves toward their cars. One driver’s vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children, and he was seeking help from his insurance company. Another woman’s vehicle stopped working minutes after she drove toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. A nearby man eventually tried to help her get out. A couple who had been stranded for about an hour described watching their vehicle sink deeper as waves from passing traffic pushed it around.

The flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman was trying to figure out how to collect her children after parents were notified that they needed to retrieve their students. She said her sister had lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year and questioned whether the city’s road-widening work was being matched by drainage improvements. The driver seeking insurance help, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have worsened after heavy rain events.

The city says it is working on longer-term drainage improvements in the Oak Hammock neighborhood. Plans include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to address recurring flooding. That project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.

In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are checking water flow and addressing potholes reported or found during inspections. Police are asking residents to avoid unnecessary travel. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

hero.headline: Indian River County declares flooding emergency, announces two shelters
hero.body:
Indian River County declared a local state of emergency Monday as continued rainfall left numerous roads impassable, and announced shelters in Sebastian and Vero Beach. County officials urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel through flooded areas, obey road closures and barricades, and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways.

The emergency order took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday and remains in effect until further order. County officials said the declaration authorizes emergency actions, coordination of response efforts and measures to address hazardous conditions as flooding and deteriorating weather continue.

The county announced a 6:30 p.m. Monday opening time for shelters at Sebastian River Middle School, 9400 Co Rd 512 in Sebastian, and Osceola Magnet School (formerly Osceola Middle School), 480 20th Ave SW, Vero Beach. The Osceola Magnet School location is pet-friendly.

Residents can report non-emergency flooding or property damage through the online reporting portal at IndianRiver.gov. For information or questions, the county’s phone number is 772-226-4000. Officials encouraged residents to monitor official county communications for updates as conditions change.

St. Lucie County also declared a local state of emergency Monday afternoon to expedite access to additional resources that may be needed. Its Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation. Public Safety personnel are coordinating with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments as crews address flooding in streets and neighborhoods. Officials asked residents to refrain from traveling Monday evening if possible and warned against driving through flooded roads.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County warned residents to avoid food or drinks contaminated by floodwater and to avoid contact with floodwater, particularly with open cuts or sores. Anyone whose wounds are exposed should wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Residents unsure whether flooding has affected a private well should use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. Health officials also advised people whose septic systems have slow plumbing to conserve water and avoid having septic tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high.

cards.headline: Flooding strands drivers on Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Water reached about knee-deep in parts of Southwest Airoso Boulevard, stalling vehicles as passing traffic pushed waves toward stranded drivers. A city drainage project in Oak Hammock could take years to complete.
cards.body:
Heavy rain stranded drivers along Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie, where floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas and covered sidewalks. Vehicles stalled as drivers tried to cross the flooded roadway, and passing cars sent waves toward those waiting for help. Port St. Lucie police are urging residents to stay home unless travel is absolutely necessary, while a city project to address recurring flooding remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.

One driver’s vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children. He was waiting on hold with his insurance company to seek help. The man, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have worsened during heavy rain events. Another woman became stranded minutes after driving toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. Water rushed toward her vehicle, and a nearby man eventually tried to help her get out. A couple stranded nearby for about an hour watched their vehicle sink deeper as waves from passing traffic pushed it around.

The flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman was trying to figure out how to retrieve her children after parents were notified to pick up their students. She said her sister had lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year. The vehicle was only three months old, she said. She questioned whether the city’s road-widening work was being matched by drainage improvements.

The city says its longer-term drainage work includes a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood. Plans call for new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to help address recurring flooding. The project is still in the data-collection phase.

For now, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are checking water flow and addressing potholes reported or found during inspections. Police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls about vehicles stranded in floodwaters. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate its depth or current.

hero.headline: Flooding moves polling sites in St. Lucie and Indian River counties for Nov. 3 election
hero.body:
Flooding-related polling changes for the Nov. 3 general election now include several St. Lucie County precincts and Indian River County Precinct 26, in addition to the previously announced move of Indian River County Precinct 7 from Sebastian Church of God to Sebastian Elks Lodge.

St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced temporary replacements for polling places affected by flooding from heavy rainfall. Voters in the affected precincts will cast their ballots at these locations:

• Precinct 12, normally at Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge: Days Inn Midtown, the Precinct 25 polling location, at 3224 S US Hwy 1 in Fort Pierce.

• Precincts 49 and 71, normally at Oak Hammock K-8 School: Port St. Lucie Community Center, the Precinct 45 polling location, at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd in Port St. Lucie.

• Precinct 51, normally at Disabled American Veterans Hall: Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd in Port St. Lucie.

• Precincts 67 and 86, normally at St. Lucie West Centennial High School: Indian River State College, Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. Voters should enter from Peacock Boulevard.

• Precinct 83, normally at Lewis Library: Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Lane in Port St. Lucie.

• Precinct 92, normally at The Brennity at Tradition: Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Lane in Port St. Lucie.

The St. Lucie County elections office said the relocations are intended to provide safe and accessible places for voters to cast their ballots.

In Indian River County, Precinct 7 voters normally assigned to Sebastian Church of God at 281 Delaware Ave. in Sebastian will instead vote at Sebastian Elks Lodge. The Indian River County Supervisor of Elections has posted an official notice about that change on its website.

Precinct 26 voters normally assigned to Morning Star Church at 689 Timber Ridge Trail SW in Vero Beach will instead vote at the Intergenerational Recreation Room (ig Center) in Vero Beach.

Election officials are encouraging affected voters to go directly to their newly assigned polling locations on Election Day.

hero.headline: Indian River County declares emergency as flooding makes numerous roads impassable
hero.body:
Indian River County declared a local state of emergency Monday as continued rainfall and flooding made numerous roads impassable. County officials urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel through flood-affected areas, obey road closures and barricades, and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways. The emergency order took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday and will remain in effect until further order.

The county issued the order in response to ongoing flooding, deteriorating weather conditions and continued rainfall. Officials said the impassable roads pose public safety concerns. The declaration gives the county authority to take emergency actions, coordinate response efforts and address hazardous conditions as they develop. Indian River County encouraged residents to monitor official county communications for updates as conditions change, saying protecting residents, visitors and emergency responders remains a priority.

St. Lucie County also declared a local state of emergency Monday afternoon to expedite access to additional resources that may be needed as flooding affects streets and neighborhoods. Its Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation. Public Safety personnel are coordinating with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments, while crews work to address flooding problems across the county. Officials asked residents to refrain from traveling Monday evening if possible and warned motorists against driving through flooded roads.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County warned residents about potential health hazards associated with floodwaters. Health officials advised people to avoid eating or drinking anything contaminated with floodwater and to avoid contact with floodwater, particularly if they have open cuts or sores. Anyone whose wounds have been exposed to floodwater should thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Health officials also warned that heavy rainfall could make water from flooded private wells unsafe to drink. Residents unsure whether flooding has affected their wells should use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing their teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. People with septic systems experiencing slow plumbing should conserve water and avoid having their septic tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high.

cards.headline: Flooding moves Indian River County Precinct 7 voting to Sebastian Elks Lodge
cards.teaser: Precinct 7 voters will cast ballots at Sebastian Elks Lodge for the Nov. 3 general election after flooding forced a move from Sebastian Church of God.
cards.body:
Indian River County voters assigned to Precinct 7 will cast their ballots at Sebastian Elks Lodge for the Nov. 3 general election after flooding forced a change in their polling location. The Indian River County Supervisor of Elections announced that the precinct’s normal voting site, Sebastian Church of God at 281 Delaware Ave. in Sebastian, will not be used because of flooding from heavy rainfall.

Affected Precinct 7 voters are being directed to the lodge in Sebastian, FL 32958. Election officials are encouraging voters whose polling places have changed to go directly to their newly assigned locations on Election Day. The Indian River County Supervisor of Elections has also posted an official notice about the Sebastian relocation on its website.

Heavy rainfall and flooding also forced the relocation of two polling places in Palm Beach County ahead of the same election. Voters in Precinct 6401 who normally cast ballots at Casa Rio Clubhouse have been reassigned to Riviera Beach Preparatory and Achievement Academy, 7071 Garden Road in Riviera Beach, FL 33404. Precinct 7628 voters who normally vote at Ironhorse Country Club will instead report to North County Senior Center, 5217 Northlake Blvd. in Palm Beach Gardens, FL 33418.

Palm Beach County election officials said affected voters will receive an email and/or text message about the polling-place changes if the elections office has their contact information. Signs will also be posted at the original polling places to direct voters to their new locations.

cards.headline: Flooding closes Port St. Lucie roads, suspends St. Lucie County's regular ART service
cards.teaser: City officials have closed several Port St. Lucie roads and are monitoring others for possible closures. St. Lucie County's regular ART transit service is temporarily suspended because of flooding and unsafe road conditions.
cards.body:
Flooding forced road closures in Port St. Lucie and temporarily suspended St. Lucie County's regular Area Regional Transit (ART) service Monday as officials urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel. The county activated its Emergency Operations Center and issued a local state of emergency as crews responded to widespread flooding and unsafe driving conditions.

City officials have closed California and Savona boulevards, as well as Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Aviation Avenue. Officials are monitoring SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard south of Gatlin Boulevard and St. Lucie West Boulevard for possible closures. Becker Road and Savona Boulevard are also being monitored. Tradition Parkway, Community Boulevard, Volucia Drive and Innovation Way remain open, though water has been reported on those roads and officials are monitoring conditions.

Police also reported flooding on Southwest Airoso Boulevard; Southeast Thornhill Drive; Southworth Boulevard and Jeanette Drive; Country Club Estates; Southwest Discovery Way and Community Boulevard in Tradition; and LTC Parkway. City crews are checking drainage systems and responding to potholes. Officials urged drivers to leave barricades in place and avoid flooded roadways. Drivers whose vehicles become stranded can call a towing company directly if they are not in immediate danger and do not require rescue.

ART officials are contacting passengers affected by the suspension and monitoring road conditions before regular transportation service resumes. County offices and schools closed early Monday because of the flooding. St. Lucie County spokesperson Eric Gill said the Emergency Operations Center is at a Level 2 partial activation. The local state of emergency gives the county access to resources if needed. Gill said road closures continue to change as conditions evolve and urged residents to stay off the roads if possible.

The National Weather Service in Melbourne said east-central Florida, including Indian River County, remains under a flood watch until 7 p.m. Forecasters expect an additional 1 to 3 inches of rain, with some locations facing a 10% chance of receiving 5 inches or more. Port St. Lucie officials encouraged residents to monitor the city's website and the Port St. Lucie Police Department's social media channels for traffic updates and potential road closures.

Lucie Police Department ( PSLPD ) is urging residents to avoid unnecessary travel as emergency crews respond to widespread flooding. Police report flooding on Southwest Airoso Boulevard, Southeast Thornhill Drive, Southworth Boulevard and Jeanette Drive, Country Club Estates, Southwest Discovery Way and Community Boulevard in Tradition, and LTC Parkway. City officials have closed California and Savona boulevards and Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Aviation Avenue, while SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard south of Gatlin Boulevard, St. Lucie West Boulevard, and Becker Road and Savona Boulevard are being monitored for possible closures as conditions worsen. "Turn around, don't drown!" police reminded residents. Officials said drivers whose vehicles become stranded in floodwaters can call a towing company directly if they are not in immediate danger and do not require rescue. Water has also been reported on Tradition Parkway, Community Boulevard, Volucia Drive, and Innovation Way, which remain open but are being monitored. City crews are checking drainage systems, responding to potholes, and urging drivers not to remove barricades or travel through flooded roadways. Motorists are being urged to avoid the intersection and use alternate routes. See also: GALLERY: Flooded roads creating challenges for drivers in Palm Beach County St. Lucie County has activated its Emergency Operations Center and issued a local state of emergency as flooding continues across the county, spokesperson Eric Gill said. "We're at a Level 2 partial activation at the Emergency Operations Center and have issued a local state of emergency to give us the means to access resources if we need them," Gill told CBS12 News on Monday. Gill said road closures continue to change as conditions evolve and urged residents to stay off the roads if possible. County offices and schools closed early Monday because of the flooding. Area Regional Transit (ART) has temporarily suspended regular transportation service due to flooding and unsafe road conditions, with officials contacting affected passengers and monitoring conditions before service resumes. For more information, visit SLCART . Lucie County schools announce early dismissal, cancel aftercare Flood watch remains in effect across the Treasure Coast According to the National Weather Service in Melbourne, east-central Florida, including Indian River County, remains under a flood watch until 7 p.m. Forecasters expect an additional 1 to 3 inches of rainfall, with some locations facing a 10% chance of receiving 5 inches or more. In Indian River County, officials are warning residents to prepare for scattered to widespread showers and thunderstorms, with periods of heavy rainfall that could lead to localized flooding of roads and low-lying areas. According to county officials, the primary weather hazards include: Heavy rainfall and localized flooding. Wind gusts of 25 to 40 mph. Dangerous beach and marine conditions. Officials said the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding could continue through Tuesday. Residents are being urged to secure loose outdoor items, allow extra travel time, slow down on wet roads and keep multiple ways to receive weather alerts. With the ground already saturated from previous rainfall, additional storms could quickly lead to standing water on roadways and worsening flooding conditions. Lucie officials are encouraging residents to monitor the city's website and the Port St. Lucie Police Department's social media channels for updates on traffic conditions and potential road closures. Okeechobee County roads remain underwater Meanwhile, several major roadways in Okeechobee County remain underwater, with officials warning that flooding could continue for several days, even after the weather improves. Authorities said warning signs have been placed in affected areas, but motorists should use extreme caution. According to county officials, the following major roads are experiencing flooding: State Road 68 East: The roadway is underwater from the 3000 block to the 15000 block. State Road 70 East: Water is covering the roadway in the 11000 block near Posey's Corner. Highway 441 North: The roadway is underwater near Potter Road. Officials stressed that these are only some of the major roads affected by flooding. Numerous local and residential streets throughout Okeechobee County also remain flooded, with some completely submerged and potentially impassable. Motorists are being warned not to assume roads outside the listed areas are safe. Floodwaters could damage roadways County officials also warned that many roads have been saturated or submerged for more than 24 hours, raising concerns about damage to pavement and underlying road structures. Prolonged exposure to floodwaters can weaken road surfaces, while standing water can conceal washouts, pavement deterioration and other hazards. Authorities said a road that was passable earlier may no longer be safe to travel. Drivers who must travel are being urged to significantly reduce their speed and avoid flooded roadways whenever possible. Officials warned that driving too fast through standing water increases the risk of hydroplaning and losing control of a vehicle. Vehicles traveling through flooded streets can also create waves that push additional water into nearby homes and properties, worsening flooding for residents. Okeechobee County residents in need of more information can contact the county call center at 863-824-6888 or the nonemergency line at 863-763-3117.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County schools to dismiss one hour early, cancel after-school activities
cards.teaser: The district's new dismissal plan follows an earlier announcement allowing voluntary pickups amid flooding. Aftercare programs are also canceled Monday.
cards.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will dismiss all students one hour early Monday and cancel all after-school activities, including aftercare, as heavy rain and flooding affect St. Lucie County. The district announced the changes after earlier allowing parents and guardians to pick up their children early.

Students will be dismissed one hour before their regularly scheduled dismissal times. Parts of the county received up to 6 inches of rain. The earlier pickup announcement excluded Oak Hammock K-8 School because of flooding in front of the school.

All student absences Monday will be excused, according to the district. Families are urged to plan for adjusted dismissal times and monitor the district's website and social media channels for updates.

Oak Hammock K-8 School is not allowing early pickups because of flooding in front of the school, according to the district. It was not immediately clear how the flooding would affect the school's updated dismissal schedule. hero.headline: Indian River, St. Lucie counties declare local emergencies as flooding inundates roads
hero.body:
Indian River County and St. Lucie County declared local states of emergency Monday as heavy rainfall flooded roads and neighborhoods across the Treasure Coast. Indian River County officials said numerous roads had become impassable, creating public safety concerns. Officials urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel Monday evening and warned motorists never to attempt to drive through flooded roads. St. Lucie County's Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation.

Indian River County's emergency order took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday and will remain in effect until further order. County officials said the declaration authorizes emergency actions, coordination of response efforts and measures to address hazardous conditions as they develop. St. Lucie County declared its emergency Monday afternoon to expedite access to additional resources that may be needed as flooding affects streets and neighborhoods.

St. Lucie County Public Safety personnel are coordinating with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments in response to the flooding. Crews are working to address problems across the county. Indian River County officials urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel through flood-affected areas and obey road closures and barricades. Both counties asked residents to monitor official sources as conditions change.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County also warned residents about potential health hazards associated with floodwaters. Health officials advised against eating or drinking anything contaminated with floodwater and urged people to avoid contact with it, particularly if they have open cuts or sores. People whose wounds have been exposed to floodwater should thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Residents with flooded private wells were advised that heavy rainfall could make their water unsafe to drink. Those unsure whether flooding has affected their wells should use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing their teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. Health officials also advised people with septic systems experiencing slow plumbing to conserve water and avoid having their septic tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high.

hero.headline: Flooding moves Indian River County Precinct 7 voting to Sebastian Elks Lodge
hero.body:
Flooding at Sebastian Church of God has prompted Indian River County election officials to move Precinct 7 voting to Sebastian Elks Lodge for the Nov. 3 general election. The church, at 281 Delaware Ave. in Sebastian, is the precinct’s usual polling place, but voters assigned there are being directed to the lodge on Fleming Street in Sebastian, FL 32958. The Indian River County Supervisor of Elections announced the switch because of flooding at the church. Officials are urging affected voters to head directly to the replacement polling location on Election Day rather than first going to their regular voting site.

The Sebastian relocation is one of several polling-place changes following heavy rainfall in Indian River and Palm Beach counties. In Indian River County, the announced change applies to voters assigned to Precinct 7, whose normal voting location is Sebastian Church of God. The county elections office has also placed an official notice about the move on its website. That notice concerns the shift from the Delaware Avenue church to Sebastian Elks Lodge. The direction for those voters is to use the lodge for the Nov. 3 election instead of the church location affected by flooding.

In Palm Beach County, flooding has forced election officials to move voting for two precincts to different Election Day locations. Voters in Precinct 6401, who usually vote at Casa Rio Clubhouse, have been reassigned to Riviera Beach Preparatory and Achievement Academy. The academy is at 7071 Garden Road in Riviera Beach, FL 33404. The other change affects Precinct 7628, which normally votes at Ironhorse Country Club. Those voters are being sent to North County Senior Center at 5217 Northlake Blvd. in Palm Beach Gardens, FL 33418. Each replacement site is tied to a specific precinct: the academy for Precinct 6401 and the senior center for Precinct 7628.

Palm Beach County election officials said affected voters will receive an email, a text message or both if the elections office has their contact information. Signs will also be placed at the original polling locations to direct voters to the replacement sites. Those notifications and signs will point voters away from the locations they ordinarily use and toward their reassigned polling places. Across the affected precincts, officials are encouraging voters to go straight to their new sites. For Indian River County’s Precinct 7, that means casting an Election Day ballot at Sebastian Elks Lodge.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie flooding strands vehicles as police urge residents to avoid travel
hero.body:
Widespread flooding stranded vehicles across Port St. Lucie on Monday and closed the intersection of Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Savona Boulevard. The Port St. Lucie Police Department urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel while emergency personnel responded to flooding in neighborhoods and on major roads.

Police said officers were responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters. They warned motorists not to underestimate the depth or movement of water covering roads. Drivers whose vehicles become stranded can contact a towing company directly if they are not in immediate danger and do not need an emergency rescue, officials said.

Police identified flooding on Southwest Airoso Boulevard; Southeast Thornhill Drive and surrounding side streets; Southworth Boulevard and Jeanette Drive; Country Club Estates; Southwest Discovery Way and Community Boulevard in Tradition; and LTC Parkway. Water also was reported on Traditional Parkway, Community Boulevard, Volucia Drive, and Innovation Way. Those roads remained open as crews and police assessed conditions.

City officials urged motorists to avoid the closed Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Savona Boulevard intersection and use alternate routes. Drivers also were warned not to remove barricades or attempt to travel through closed roads. Crews were checking drainage systems to ensure water was flowing properly and addressing potholes found or reported throughout the area. The city advised residents who encounter potholes to avoid the affected area and call 911.

The National Weather Service in Melbourne said east-central Florida, including Indian River County, remained under a flood watch until 7 p.m. Forecasters expected another 1 to 3 inches of rain, with some locations facing a 10% chance of receiving at least 5 inches. Indian River County officials warned that periods of heavy rainfall could flood roads and low-lying areas, with the potential for heavy rain and flooding continuing through Tuesday.

Port St. Lucie officials encouraged residents to monitor the city's website and the Port St. Lucie Police Department's social media channels for traffic conditions and potential road closures. Residents with questions about school closures were advised to contact their schools directly. Officials reminded motorists that a road that was passable earlier may no longer be safe.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools allows early pickups Monday amid flooding concerns
cards.teaser: Parents and guardians may pick up students immediately, except at Oak Hammock K-8 School because of flooding in front of the school. All Monday student absences will be excused.
cards.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools is allowing parents and guardians to pick up their children early Monday, Nov. 2, amid flooding concerns. Families who wish to pick up their children may do so immediately, the district announced.

Oak Hammock K-8 School is excluded from the early-pickup option because of flooding in front of the school. The district also announced that all student absences on Monday will be excused.

Parents and guardians are encouraged to monitor the district’s social media accounts and website for additional updates.

hero.headline: Police urge drivers to avoid flooded St. Lucie West as vehicles become stranded
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department is urging drivers to avoid flooded portions of St. Lucie West unless travel is absolutely necessary as officers respond to reports of stranded vehicles. Police said high water has made several roads difficult to navigate and created hazardous conditions.

Drivers should not attempt to cross standing water, police said. Motorists who encounter flooding are being advised to turn around and find an alternate route. “Never underestimate the depth or power of floodwaters,” the department said in a news release. Residents are also being asked to stay off the roads if possible and give emergency responders room to work.

Officers are continuing to monitor conditions and will provide updates as road closures and other traffic impacts develop, police said. The flooding comes amid heavy rain affecting the Treasure Coast, with areas receiving repeated rounds of downpours.

hero.headline: Martin County early voting ends; Election Day voters must use assigned precincts
hero.body:
Martin County voters who plan to cast a ballot in person in Tuesday’s General Election must go to their assigned precinct now that early voting has ended. The county’s early voting period closed Saturday, with about 29,000 people having voted early. Election workers finished the final day at the Martin County Supervisor of Elections Office in Stuart. County officials said more than 40% of registered voters had already voted, combining ballots cast early and by mail. That share has already surpassed the county’s overall turnout of 29% in the primary, before any Election Day votes are added.

Knowing where to vote is election officials’ main concern heading into Tuesday. Martin County voters can look up their assigned polling location at MartinVotes.gov or call 772-288-5637 for help finding it. With early voting over, Election Day is the only remaining opportunity to vote in person, and voters must use their designated precinct rather than choose an early voting location. The location lookup and phone number give voters two ways to check where they need to go before heading out to cast a ballot. “We've had a great turnout in Martin County,” Vicki Davis said.

Voters who still have vote-by-mail ballots can return them to county elections offices during business hours Monday. The final deadline for returning those ballots is 7 p.m. Tuesday. Election officials do not use postmarks to determine whether ballots meet the deadline, so voters need to ensure their ballots are returned on time. Voting by mail is an option statewide, alongside early voting and voting in person on Election Day. Across Florida, about 1.8 million vote-by-mail ballots have been counted. Separately, more than 2.8 million of the state’s 13.7 million registered voters have already cast ballots through early voting.

Early voting also ended Saturday elsewhere on the Treasure Coast and in Okeechobee County. St. Lucie County recorded nearly 56,000 early voters, while Indian River County had about 29,000, roughly the same total as Martin County. More than 3,700 people voted early in Okeechobee County. Palm Beach County’s schedule extended a day longer, allowing residents to vote Sunday at any of its 28 early voting sites. Nearly 178,000 people had voted early in Palm Beach County. Nationally, more than 50 million ballots had been cast ahead of Election Day, with Florida’s early and mail voting totals contributing to that nationwide count.

hero.headline: Camry left lane, hit parked truck in fatal I-95 crash in Martin County
hero.body:
A Toyota Camry left its lane and struck a tractor-trailer parked on the shoulder of I-95 in northern Martin County in a crash that killed three passengers late Saturday, the Florida Highway Patrol said in details released Sunday morning. Northbound lanes reopened after 5 a.m. following an hourslong closure.

The crash happened around 11:05 p.m. at mile marker 112. The Camry was traveling north in the outside lane when it moved onto the right paved shoulder, where the tractor-trailer was parked, according to FHP. The front right of the Camry struck the rear left of the tractor-trailer. The car then rotated across all three lanes and stopped on the left paved shoulder.

The passengers killed were a 34-year-old man and a 5-year-old boy, both from Port St. Lucie, and a woman. The Camry’s driver, a 31-year-old woman from Port St. Lucie, was taken by ground to St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach. An 11-year-old girl suffered incapacitating injuries and was transported by helicopter.

All northbound lanes at mile marker 112 were closed after the crash, and traffic was diverted off I-95 at SW Martin Highway. Martin County Fire Rescue and the Martin County Sheriff’s Office also responded to the scene.

cards.headline: Unsafe bacteria levels prompt water advisory at 10 Martin County locations
cards.teaser: Health officials urge people to avoid water contact at 10 Martin County locations. The health department plans to resample Monday if conditions allow.
cards.body:
The Department of Health in Martin County has issued a health advisory after water samples taken Monday showed unsafe levels of fecal bacteria at 10 locations across the county. Health officials are urging beachgoers to stay out of the water this weekend and avoid contact with it, saying exposure could increase the risk of illness in swimmers. The advisory followed poor water quality results in several areas of Martin County.

Beach conditions Friday included choppy water and a red flag flying, alongside the water quality concerns. For some beachgoers, the rough surf was enough to keep them out of the water. “You know, it's not safe to swim in the water, especially at this time of year when you want to be in the water,” beachgoer Dan Casamento said. Valentin Kapranoe, a snowbird who had just learned about the advisory, also expressed concern. “I would be a little bit concerned for sure,” Kapranoe said.

Officials say the poor water quality is likely tied to recent wind, king tides and stormwater runoff from heavy rain. Beachgoer Charlene Cook described the situation as disappointing, particularly for people visiting the area. “What a shame especially if you're vacationing,” Cook said. She also expressed concern about the broader environmental effects of runoff. “What bothers me the most is the runoff from the lawns and the lawn treatments and what it does to the environment,” she said.

The health department plans to resample the water Monday if conditions allow. Officials expect water quality to stabilize as the weather clears.

hero.headline: Three killed, including 5-year-old boy, in I-95 crash in Martin County
hero.body:
Three people, including a 5-year-old boy, were killed and an 11-year-old girl was seriously injured when a car struck a parked tractor-trailer on northbound Interstate 95 in Martin County late Saturday night, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.

The crash was reported around 11:05 p.m. Investigators said a 2017 Toyota Camry was traveling in the outside northbound lane when it moved onto the right shoulder and struck the rear of a 53-foot trailer attached to a parked 2012 Kenworth tractor-trailer. The impact sent the Camry spinning across all three northbound lanes before it came to rest on the left shoulder.

The three people killed were passengers in the Camry: a 34-year-old man, the 5-year-old boy and a woman. The driver, a 31-year-old Port St. Lucie woman, suffered non-incapacitating injuries and was transported by ground. The 11-year-old girl, also a passenger in the car, suffered incapacitating injuries and was flown by LifeStar.

The tractor-trailer was parked on the right shoulder at the time of the collision. Its driver, a 60-year-old Miami man, was uninjured. The Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the crash.

hero.headline: Broward County man jailed after reported assault at Fort Pierce hotel
hero.body:
Deputies arrested a Broward County man after a reported assault at a Fort Pierce hotel, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Guyrson Maddy, 37, is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a domestic battery charge, with Broward County holds for probation violations in four felony cases.

Deputies were called to the Best Western in the 7900 block of South U.S. Highway 1 around 11:20 p.m. Friday. A witness reported seeing a man assault a woman, push her into a vehicle and drive away. Deputies confirmed a battery had occurred and identified Maddy as the suspect, the sheriff’s office said. A records check found an active warrant for probation violations in four separate felony cases dating from 2017 to 2025.

Investigators identified a dark-colored 2025 Tesla Model Y they believed was involved. Deputies found a vehicle matching that description at a home on Palm Breezes Drive. A woman at the home confirmed she had been at the hotel and directed deputies to a bathroom, where they found Maddy.

Deputy Mendoza and his K-9 partner, Oso, helped find Maddy. He followed deputies’ commands and was arrested without incident, according to the sheriff’s office.

hero.headline: Florida voters to decide homestead tax exemption increases Tuesday
hero.body:
Florida voters will decide three statewide amendments Tuesday, including a proposal to increase the homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. The other measures address the state's budget stabilization fund and property taxes on agricultural equipment.

The homestead proposal, Amendment 3, has drawn the most attention. Supporters say it would provide relief for homeowners and limit government spending. Opponents warn it could reduce local government revenue. All three amendments require 60% approval to pass.

Amendment 1 would increase Florida's budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% and require annual transfers into the fund of up to $750 million. Lawmakers could use those reserves for certain critical state needs. Supporters say the measure would strengthen the state's financial safety net, while critics argue the money would be better spent addressing current needs.

Amendment 2 would exempt agricultural equipment and other farm-related tangible personal property from property taxes. Supporters say the exemption would help farmers and the agriculture industry. Opponents say it could reduce revenue for local services.

Early voting ended Saturday in Martin and Okeechobee counties. It wraps up Sunday in St. Lucie, Indian River and Palm Beach counties. Election Day polls will be open Tuesday from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

hero.headline: Man arrested in Fort Pierce after reported assault at South U.S. Highway 1 hotel
hero.body:

Deputies also found outstanding Broward County warrants for probation violations.

Deputies responded to the Best Western in the 7900 block of South U.S. Highway 1 at approximately 11:20 p.m. Friday. A witness reported seeing a man physically assault a woman, push her into a vehicle and leave the area. Deputies confirmed that a battery had occurred and identified Maddy as the suspect, according to the Sheriff’s Office.

The investigation led deputies about 15 miles northwest of the hotel as they searched for a dark-colored 2025 Tesla Model Y believed to have been involved in the incident. They found a vehicle matching that description at a residence on Palm Breezes Drive in Fort Pierce.

A woman at the residence confirmed she had been at the hotel and directed deputies to a bathroom. A deputy and his K-9 partner located Maddy there. Deputies apprehended him without incident and took him to the St. Lucie County Jail on the domestic battery charge.

The Broward County probation-violation holds involve battery on a law enforcement officer, fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, grand theft, criminal use of personal identification information, defrauding an innkeeper and driving while license revoked.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie woman arrested on 29 animal-cruelty counts after 124 cats found in home
hero.body:
Kimberly K. Robinson, 66, of Port St. Lucie, was arrested Friday on 29 counts of cruelty to animals after investigators found 124 cats, including some that were deceased, inside her home, according to PSLPD. Detectives obtained an arrest warrant before taking Robinson into custody.

The investigation began Oct. 13, when Animal Control responded to a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street over concerns about animal welfare and unsanitary living conditions. More than 60 cats were discovered inside during the initial response, police said.

Officers observed extensive accumulations of animal urine and feces, an ammonia odor, and several cats suffering from untreated medical conditions. Multiple visits to the home brought the total to 124 cats of all ages, according to police. Many of the cats required veterinary attention for numerous medical conditions.

The cats were divided between Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County after Animal Control reached capacity, police said. The investigation remains active.

hero.headline: State review finds no statistically significant glioblastoma excess in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Florida health officials released an updated brain cancer review Thursday that found no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in St. Lucie County or the three ZIP codes examined. The assessment covers diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, with additional analysis of ZIP codes 34952, 34983 and 34982. Its focus on glioblastoma and ZIP-code totals leaves Fort Pierce families seeking a closer examination of other brain tumors and patients who lived on the same streets.

In St. Lucie County, officials recorded 95 glioblastoma diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, ZIP code 34952 had 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected; 34983 had 21, compared with approximately 20 expected; and 34982 had 12, compared with approximately 13 expected. The comparisons used statewide cancer rates and accounted for age. Officials said small case counts can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without increasing the underlying risk.

Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast, wants officials to examine smaller areas within the ZIP codes. She has pointed to Fort Pierce homes where she said brain tumor patients lived only doors apart. Her husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012, and Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. She is now helping Amber Lee, 37, who has oligodendroglioma and grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Cunningham. Their shared initial diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. Lee wants officials to continue studying local brain tumor diagnoses.

The updated review excludes oligodendroglioma, a distinct brain tumor. The department said evolving medical classifications place two codes used in its 2019 analysis, 9450 and 9451, outside the current glioblastoma definition. The review ends with 2023, the latest finalized cancer registry year, because records undergo checks for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis came after that period. The assessment uses ZIP-code totals rather than examining concentrations on individual streets. The Florida Cancer Data System generally records addresses at diagnosis rather than complete residential histories or detailed exposure information, limiting what those addresses can establish about earlier residences or potentially relevant exposures. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners.
hero.article_text: Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma Ankiel said she was not surprised by the state’s conclusion. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. Her questions are also personal. Ankiel’s husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012. Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Now, Ankiel is helping another patient with the same initial diagnosis. Amber Lee, 37, is living with oligodendroglioma, a brain tumor that is distinct from glioblastoma. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination. The state analyzed entire ZIP codes, not individual streets. Maybe the ZIP codes are a little bit too broad, Ankiel said. Let’s actually, let’s look at some of the streets. Why oligodendroglioma was not counted The updated review focuses specifically on glioblastoma. It excludes oligodendroglioma the tumor Lee is living with and the tumor Ankiel said her husband was initially diagnosed with. The report shows two tumor classification codes included in the state’s 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes are no longer included in the current glioblastoma definition. The I-Team previously asked health officials how their analysis handles patients whose diagnoses change and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. The report does not explain how a case initially classified as oligodendroglioma and later diagnosed as glioblastoma would be counted. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. The review also does not capture more recent glioblastoma diagnoses previously covered by the I-Team. Lucie resident Laura Cooper told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Street-level limitations The report acknowledges limitations in the Florida Cancer Data System. The registry generally records a patient’s address at the time of diagnosis. It does not contain a complete residential history or detailed information about possible environmental exposures. That means a patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where that person lived years earlier or where a potentially relevant exposure occurred. The report also does not analyze whether cases are concentrated on individual streets or within smaller sections of the ZIP codes examined. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The scientific journal article provided by the department is a broader review of existing research into environmental hazards and brain tumors. It is not a study of Treasure Coast patients, neighborhoods or environmental conditions. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners. Ankiel said she is not trying to work against health officials and wants to work with them. But for the families she has met, the state’s statistical conclusion does not resolve the questions raised by patients living in the same neighborhoods or sometimes only a few houses apart.

hero.headline: Martin County man charged with attempted murder after roommate’s neck slashed
hero.body:
Bradley Martin, 32, was arrested Thursday night on an attempted murder charge after deputies say he slashed his roommate’s neck with a box cutter, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.

Despite his injuries, the victim attempted to drive himself to a hospital, authorities said. Deputies and Fire Rescue personnel intercepted him and took him to a trauma hospital.

The victim was in stable condition and is expected to recover, according to the sheriff’s office.

hero.headline: Flooding forces cancellation of Nov. 7 St. Lucie County 4-H Fall Festival
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County 4-H Fall Festival scheduled for Nov. 7 has been canceled after flooding left the 4-H Farm grounds waterlogged, organizers said. They said holding the festival could pose safety risks for vendors, volunteers, families and attendees.

The county announced the cancellation Friday on Instagram. With more rain in the forecast, organizers said there was too little time for conditions to improve. They expressed disappointment and thanked those who had volunteered, participated or sponsored the event.

Residents can still support 4-H youth by donating peanut butter and canned goods. Drop-off locations include UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County, 8400 Picos Road, and Morningside Library.
